syntax_error:
-- Look just before "{token}": a missing comma, an unclosed ' or ( , or MySQL-only syntax.
-- PostgreSQL: 'single quotes' for text, "double quotes" only for names, no `backticks`; LIMIT n OFFSET m (not LIMIT m, n).
unknown_table: SELECT table_schema, table_name FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_name ILIKE '%{table_hint}%';

-- Check the schema/search_path too:
SHOW search_path;
unknown_column: SELECT column_name FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_name = '{table}';
-- A text value in "double quotes" is read as a column name: use 'single quotes' for text.
ambiguous_column:
-- Put the table (or its alias) in front of the column:
SELECT t1.{column}, ... FROM t1 JOIN t2 ON ... WHERE t1.{column} = ...;
unknown_function: -- PostgreSQL equivalents: GROUP_CONCAT -> STRING_AGG(col, ','), IFNULL -> COALESCE, DATE_FORMAT -> TO_CHAR, or add an explicit ::type cast to the arguments
group_by_strict:
SELECT customer_id, MAX(customer_name) AS customer_name, SUM(total)
FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id;
duplicate_key:
-- See the row that already has it:
SELECT * FROM {table} WHERE {column} = '{value}';

-- Save without failing when it already exists (upsert):
INSERT INTO {table} ({column}, ...) VALUES (...)
ON CONFLICT ({column}) DO UPDATE SET ... = EXCLUDED....;   -- or DO NOTHING

-- Only for an id after an import: move the sequence past the data
SELECT setval(pg_get_serial_sequence('{table}', 'id'), (SELECT MAX(id) FROM {table}));
fk_missing_parent: -- Create the {parent} row first, or use an existing one.
not_null: ALTER TABLE {table} ALTER COLUMN {column} SET DEFAULT <value>;
-- or send a value for {column} from the app
value_too_long: ALTER TABLE {table} ALTER COLUMN {column} TYPE varchar(255);  -- or text (no length limit in PostgreSQL)
out_of_range: ALTER TABLE {table} ALTER COLUMN {column} TYPE bigint;  -- or numeric(15,2) for money
bad_value_type:
-- Send a real {token}: numbers without commas, dates as 'YYYY-MM-DD', NULL (not '') when empty.
-- To read '{value}' as a date: to_date('{value}', 'DD-MM-YYYY')
check_violation: SELECT pg_get_constraintdef(oid) FROM pg_constraint WHERE conname = '{constraint}';
charset_mismatch: -- Set the client/app connection to UTF8: SET client_encoding = 'UTF8';
disk_full:
SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_database_size(current_database()));
SELECT relname, pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size(relid)) FROM pg_catalog.pg_statio_user_tables ORDER BY pg_total_relation_size(relid) DESC LIMIT 10;

-- Check WAL: a stuck replication slot or failing archive_command keeps WAL forever:
SELECT slot_name, active FROM pg_replication_slots;

-- Common mistake: deleting files in pg_wal by hand, or running pg_resetwal to 'free space'.
-- Those files are needed to recover after a crash; removing them can leave the database unable to start or with silently inconsistent data.
-- Free space elsewhere (old logs, backups) first, fix why WAL is kept, and let PostgreSQL remove it at the next CHECKPOINT.
out_of_memory: SHOW shared_buffers; SHOW work_mem; SHOW max_connections;
-- work_mem is per sort, per connection: keep it modest (e.g. 16MB) and pool connections; shared_buffers ~25% of RAM.
packet_too_large: -- Split the statement into batches; keep big files outside the database (store a path).
statement_timeout: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) <your query>;  -- look for Seq Scan on a big table
-- Add the index the plan is missing; paste the query here and I'll write it.
deadlock: SELECT deadlocks FROM pg_stat_database WHERE datname = current_database();
-- In code: update rows in the same order (ORDER BY id ... FOR UPDATE) and retry on error 40P01.
lock_wait:
SELECT pid, pg_blocking_pids(pid) AS blocked_by, state, now() - xact_start AS running, query
FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE cardinality(pg_blocking_pids(pid)) > 0;
-- If a forgotten transaction blocks: SELECT pg_terminate_backend(<blocking pid>);  (after checking what it is)
serialization_failure: -- Retry the whole transaction 2-3 times with a short wait on error 40001.
idle_transaction: SELECT pid, now() - xact_start AS open_for, query FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state = 'idle in transaction' ORDER BY xact_start;
SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '60s';  -- per role/database: ALTER ROLE app SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '60s';
metadata_lock: SELECT pid, state, query FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE wait_event_type = 'Lock';

-- Run the ALTER with a short lock wait:
SET lock_timeout = '5s';
access_denied: -- and update the same password in the app's config
too_many_connections:
SHOW max_connections;
SELECT count(*), state FROM pg_stat_activity GROUP BY state;

-- Real fix: PgBouncer (transaction pooling) in front, and close idle connections:
ALTER ROLE app SET idle_session_timeout = '10min';
server_unreachable:
-- On the database server:
systemctl status postgresql
ss -ltnp | grep 5432
-- For remote access: listen_addresses = '*' (postgresql.conf), a pg_hba.conf line for the app server, and the firewall open for 5432 from that server only.
connection_lost: SELECT pg_postmaster_start_time();  -- recent = the server restarted
-- In the app/pool: enable pre-ping / reconnect on stale connections.
permission_denied:
GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON {table} TO <app role>;  -- only what is missing
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA public TO <app role>;
replica_lag:
-- On the primary: how far each standby is behind
SELECT application_name, client_addr, state, write_lag, flush_lag, replay_lag FROM pg_stat_replication;

-- write_lag high = the network; replay_lag high while write/flush lag are low = the standby can't apply fast enough
-- (busy disk, long queries delaying replay, or one huge transaction on the primary: batch big changes).
replication_stopped:
-- Logical replication: the subscriber's apply worker fails on that row and keeps restarting. On the subscriber:
SELECT subname, apply_error_count, sync_error_count FROM pg_stat_subscription_stats;   -- PostgreSQL 15+
-- the server log's CONTEXT line shows the table ({table}) and the change that failed

-- Make the subscriber's row match the publisher (a duplicate key: remove or fix the row that was written on the subscriber, after a backup);
-- the worker retries by itself and continues.

-- Common mistake: ALTER SUBSCRIPTION ... SKIP (lsn = ...) as the routine fix. It throws that whole transaction away on the subscriber,
-- so the two databases differ from then on. Use it only when you know the change must not be applied.
source_log_purged:
-- The standby needs WAL the primary has already deleted. Unless that WAL is in your WAL archive (restore_command), the standby can't continue:
-- rebuild it with a fresh pg_basebackup from the primary.

-- Careful: a slot whose standby is gone keeps WAL forever and can fill the disk. Drop slots you no longer use:
-- SELECT pg_drop_replication_slot('<unused slot>');
write_on_replica: SELECT pg_is_in_recovery() AS is_standby, current_setting('default_transaction_read_only') AS read_only_default, current_setting('transaction_read_only') AS read_only_now;

-- is_standby = true: you're connected to a standby; send writes to the primary (check the host in the app's config, or use target_session_attrs=read-write in the connection string).
-- read_only_default = on: the database or user was set read-only (ALTER DATABASE/ROLE ... SET default_transaction_read_only = on); find who set it before changing it back.
-- After a failover, recycle the app's connection pool so it stops using connections to the old primary.
standby_query_conflict:
-- On the standby: which kind of conflict keeps cancelling queries
SELECT datname, confl_snapshot, confl_lock, confl_bufferpin, confl_deadlock FROM pg_stat_database_conflicts;

-- Retry short queries. For long reports on the standby pick one trade-off (postgresql.conf on the standby, then reload):
-- hot_standby_feedback = on             -> queries aren't cancelled for old row versions, but the primary keeps dead rows longer (bloat)
-- max_standby_streaming_delay = 5min    -> queries get more time, but this standby falls further behind
-- 'User was holding a relation lock for too long' = the primary ran TRUNCATE/DROP/ALTER on a table the query was reading: schedule those outside report hours.
wal_retained_by_slot:
-- If the consumer is still needed, fix it so it catches up instead of dropping its slot. Add a safety limit (postgresql.conf, then reload):
-- max_slot_wal_keep_size = 50GB   -- a slot further behind than this is invalidated instead of filling the disk
wal_archive_failing:
SELECT archived_count, last_archived_wal, last_archived_time, failed_count, last_failed_wal, last_failed_time FROM pg_stat_archiver;
SHOW archive_command;

-- Read the server log line after 'archive command failed' (DETAIL shows the command), then run that command by hand as the postgres user
-- with one waiting file to see the real error: full or unmounted backup disk, wrong path, permissions, an expired cloud key.

-- Once the command works again, PostgreSQL archives the backlog by itself and removes the old files.
-- Common mistake: archive_command = '/bin/true' (or deleting .ready files) to make it 'pass'. WAL is then thrown away unarchived
-- and your backups can no longer restore past that point; if you must stop archiving, turn archive_mode off and take a new base backup later.
checkpoints_too_frequent:
ALTER SYSTEM SET max_wal_size = '4GB';   -- size it for your busiest hour; needs that much free disk headroom
SELECT pg_reload_conf();
-- Common mistake: lowering max_wal_size to save disk. It makes checkpoints even more frequent and usually writes MORE WAL (full-page writes after each checkpoint).

unknown_table.sql: SELECT table_name FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema NOT IN ('pg_catalog','information_schema')

unknown_column.sql: SELECT column_name FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_name = :table

resolve.sql: SELECT c.conrelid::regclass::text, a.attname FROM pg_constraint c JOIN pg_attribute a ON a.attrelid = c.conrelid AND a.attnum = ANY(c.conkey) WHERE c.conname = :key LIMIT 1
SELECT c.confrelid::regclass::text, a.attname FROM pg_constraint c JOIN pg_attribute a ON a.attrelid = c.confrelid AND a.attnum = ANY(c.confkey) WHERE c.conname = :constraint LIMIT 1

value_too_long.sql: SELECT character_maximum_length FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_name = :table AND column_name = :column

deadlock.sql: SELECT deadlocks FROM pg_stat_database WHERE datname = current_database()

lock_wait.sql: SELECT pid, now() - xact_start AS running, query FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE cardinality(pg_blocking_pids(pid)) > 0

idle_transaction.sql: SELECT pid, now() - xact_start AS open_for FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state = 'idle in transaction' AND now() - xact_start > interval '60 seconds'

write_on_replica.proof: this server only accepts reads (a standby, or read-only is the default)

wal_retained_by_slot.sql: SELECT slot_name, active, pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn)) FROM pg_replication_slots WHERE restart_lsn IS NOT NULL AND (NOT active OR pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn) > 1073741824)
wal_retained_by_slot.proof: replication slot(s) holding WAL with no reader or more than 1 GB behind: {rows}

wal_archive_failing.sql: SELECT last_failed_wal FROM pg_stat_archiver WHERE last_failed_time IS NOT NULL AND (last_archived_time IS NULL OR last_failed_time > last_archived_time)
wal_archive_failing.proof: WAL archiving is failing now (last failed file: {rows})

refuses.fix_en: Leave the name bare (plain names), or put it in double quotes when it is a reserved word or has spaces; a double-quoted name keeps its exact upper/lower case, a bare one is matched in lower case.
refuses.fix_hi: Naam bina quote ke likho, ya double quotes mein (double quotes mein naam ka case waisa hi rehta hai).

refuses.title_en: {db} has no LIMIT offset, count (that's MySQL/MariaDB)
refuses.title_hi: {db} mein LIMIT offset, count nahi hota
refuses.fix_en: Write LIMIT count OFFSET offset (this also works on MySQL/MariaDB).
refuses.fix_hi: LIMIT count OFFSET offset likho (ye MySQL/MariaDB pe bhi chalta hai).
CURRENT_DATE likho (MySQL/MariaDB pe bhi chalta hai).

refuses.fix_en: Use EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM now()) (seconds, with a fraction).
Use to_char(col, 'YYYY-MM-DD'); its format codes differ (%Y -> YYYY, %m -> MM, %d -> DD, %H -> HH24, %i -> MI).
refuses.fix_hi: to_char(col, 'YYYY-MM-DD') likho; format code alag hain (%Y -> YYYY, %m -> MM, %d -> DD).

refuses.title_en: {db} has no TOP n (that's SQL Server)
refuses.title_hi: {db} mein TOP n nahi hota (wo SQL Server ka hai)
refuses.fix_en: Remove TOP n and end the query with ORDER BY ... LIMIT n.
refuses.fix_hi: TOP n hatao aur aakhir mein ORDER BY ... LIMIT n likho.

refuses.fix_en: Use now() (or CURRENT_DATE for the date only).
refuses.fix_hi: now() (ya sirf date ke liye CURRENT_DATE) likho.

sum_boolean.says: PostgreSQL refuses it (42883, function sum(boolean) does not exist): a comparison is a boolean there, not a number.

having_alias.says: PostgreSQL refuses it (42703, column does not exist; or 42803 if the name is also a real column): HAVING is worked out before SELECT names exist.

count_distinct_multi.says: PostgreSQL refuses it (42883, function count(...) does not exist): COUNT takes one argument there.

window_over_ungrouped.says: PostgreSQL refuses it (42803, must appear in the GROUP BY clause or be used in an aggregate function).
